clue.text: Military officer has novel idea — do a bunk!

indicators.note: novel means new or fresh, so the word idea is given a new arrangement

parts.note: do a bunk is British slang for running off, which is to decamp

explanation.surface: An army officer comes up with a fresh plan: run away!
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges IDEA into AIDE; DECAMP follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An aide-de-camp is an officer serving as personal assistant to a senior commander.

clue.text: Belonging to the stars on the wrong track, almost getting left behind

indicators.note: behind says the letter for left comes at the end
almost means nearly all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: astray means off course

explanation.surface: Something celestial has gone off course and someone lags behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims ASTRAY to ASTRA, with L put 'behind'.
explanation.definitionFit: Astral means relating to or coming from the heavenly bodies.

clue.text: Give junk to Edna

indicators.note: junk means rubbish, so the letters are treated as scrap to be remade

explanation.surface: Hand your rubbish over to a woman called Edna.
explanation.walkthrough: 'junk' rearranges TO EDNA.
explanation.definitionFit: To give money or goods to a cause is to contribute them.

clue.text: I rang tradesmen after confusion and disorder

indicators.note: after confusion means once mixed up, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone phoned the workmen once things got muddled and messy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after confusion' rearranges I RANG TRADESMEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Being messed up or untidy is a state of upset and chaos.

clue.text: Young horse stands on this plant

parts.note: a colt is a young male horse
what the horse stands on is its foot, giving the possessive s and foot

explanation.surface: A foal plants its hoof on this weed.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant's name read in two parts is the foot of a young horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Coltsfoot is a yellow-flowered weed of the daisy family.

clue.text: Fellow getting American lists on computer screen

parts.note: the setter takes fellow loosely for men, the plural of man; strictly the singular gives only one man
US is short for United States, hence American

explanation.surface: A man with an American sees options displayed on a monitor.
explanation.walkthrough: Strictly 'Fellow' gives MAN; the wordplay needs the plural MEN, a loose touch by the setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Software shows options to choose from in drop-down panels.

clue.text: Notice a maiden and a man in the garden

parts.note: a notice is an advertisement, an ad
M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: Spot a young woman and a man together in a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden in cricket is an over with no runs scored, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible's first man lived in the Garden of Eden.

clue.text: Secretly planned deed pal and I contrived

indicators.note: contrived means artificially arranged, so the letters are set out anew

explanation.surface: A scheme hatched by two friends over a legal document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contrived' rearranges DEED PAL and I.
explanation.definitionFit: A scheme carefully worked out in advance and kept hidden is crafty and thorough.

clue.text: As a teacher, I am spinning around with nervous tension

indicators.note: spinning around says the contraction is turned to face the other way

parts.note: I am contracts to I'm
nervous tension is stress

explanation.surface: A frazzled teacher describes being in a whirl of anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spinning around' turns IM into MI.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolmistress is a female schoolteacher.

clue.text: Abbess takes Maureen on the river, then the lake

parts.note: Mo is a pet form of Maureen
taken as written
Lake Superior is one of the North American Great Lakes

explanation.surface: A nun takes a friend boating down a river and across a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbess heads a convent, a post also given the title of a senior nun.

clue.text: Sit back letting peacekeepers enter capital city

indicators.note: enter tells us the peacekeepers go inside the turned word
back says the word sit is read from its end to its start

parts.note: taken as written
the UN (United Nations) supplies peacekeeping forces

explanation.surface: Relax and let the blue helmets march into a capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns SIT into TIS, and 'enter' puts UN inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunis is the capital of Tunisia in North Africa.

clue.text: City dwellers can be solitary types, academic admitted

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so the academic is placed within the solitary types

parts.note: people who keep to themselves are loners
a don is a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: Urban folk may be isolated people, a university man among them.
explanation.definitionFit: People who live in the British capital are its residents.

clue.text: Star worker needing a short breather

parts.note: a worker ant is the crossword's standard worker

indicators.note: short means cut off at the end, so the breather loses its last letter

parts.note: a breather is a rest or pause

explanation.surface: A celebrity employee needs a quick break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims REST to RES.
explanation.definitionFit: Antares is the bright red star in the constellation Scorpius.

clue.text: One learning about the sun — small child enthralled

indicators.note: enthralled means held captive, so the child is held inside the adjective

parts.note: solar means relating to the sun
CH is a standard short form of child, small signalling the abbreviation

explanation.surface: A young pupil is captivated by astronomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about the sun' is not a container signal but the adjective SOLAR; 'enthralled' puts CH inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A scholar is a student or pupil, someone engaged in study.

clue.text: Wandering up to "arrivals", find evidence for aircraft flying

indicators.note: wandering means roaming about, so the letters of the following words stray into a new order

explanation.surface: Drifting towards the arrivals hall, someone spots signs of planes overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wandering' rearranges the twelve letters of UP TO ARRIVALS.
explanation.definitionFit: Condensation trails left high in the sky show where jets have passed.

clue.text: Showing fanaticism, I ban dress that's unsuitable

indicators.note: unsuitable means not right, so the letters are put into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: A zealot forbids an inappropriate outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unsuitable' rearranges I BAN DRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Extreme, unreasoning zeal is a mark of the frenzied, as of a mad dog.

clue.text: A badly behaved child, boy kept in for being irritating

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: kept in, like a pupil in detention, means the boy is held inside the child

parts.note: a brat is a naughty child
Dan is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A naughty child gets detention after school for being annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kept in' puts DAN inside BRAT.
explanation.definitionFit: An abradant wears surfaces away by rubbing, so it is abrasive.

clue.text: Pampered group coming in made themselves comfortable

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so the group goes inside the other word

parts.note: cose is an old verb meaning to make oneself cosy
a set is a group

explanation.surface: A spoilt crowd arrives and settles in snugly.
explanation.walkthrough: COSED is from Chambers' verb 'cose', to make oneself cosy; 'coming in' puts SET inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone cosseted has been coddled and spoilt.

clue.text: Caused a fight, involving rude baronet

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so the baronet abbreviation wraps round the word for rude

parts.note: rude can mean rough, crude or unpolished
a bout is a boxing match

explanation.surface: Started a brawl involving an ill-mannered titled gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: A baronet is a British hereditary title, abbreviated Bt; 'involving' puts ROUGH inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To have made something happen is to have produced or effected it.

clue.text: Dead snake seen outside shelter

indicators.note: outside says the snake goes around the shelter

parts.note: an asp is a venomous snake
lee is the sheltered side, away from the wind

explanation.surface: A lifeless serpent found around a refuge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead' here means numb or unfeeling, as a limb that has gone to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead leg is one that has gone numb, just like a sleeping foot.

clue.text: Communicate in writing when Henry gets in a twist

indicators.note: gets in says the letter for Henry enters the word

parts.note: to communicate in writing is to write
H is the abbreviation for henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Henry squirms while trying to send a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets in' puts H, the symbol for the henry, inside WRITE.
explanation.definitionFit: To writhe is to squirm and contort the body.

clue.text: Takes in fools without hesitation

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the fools go round the hesitation

parts.note: asses are foolish people
um is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: Tricks idiots without pausing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but here means outside, putting UM inside ASSES.
explanation.definitionFit: To take on a role or responsibility is to adopt it.

clue.text: Spare container for rubbish around end of farm

indicators.note: around says the rubbish container goes about the letter

parts.note: a skip is a large open British builders' bin for rubbish

indicators.note: end of picks the final letter of farm

explanation.surface: A spare bin for waste sits at the edge of the farmyard.
explanation.walkthrough: A SKIP is a large open metal bin, hired in Britain for building rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: To skimp is to be sparing or stingy, using too little.

clue.text: What the queen's personal servant may do with a piece of furniture

definitions.text: What the queen's personal servant may do with a piece of furniture

parts.words: What the queen's personal servant may do with a piece of furniture
parts.note: a royal attendant who helps the monarch with her clothes shares a name with a kitchen cabinet with shelves

explanation.surface: A royal servant handling some furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word names the servant who helps someone dress and a cabinet with shelves for crockery; read as wordplay, the clue says the servant 'is' the furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a valet who handles clothes and a sideboard with shelves go by this name.

clue.text: At camp under canvas I have to be alert

parts.note: taken as written
to camp under canvas is to tent
taken as written
have contracts to 've, as in I've

explanation.surface: When camping in a tent, I must stay watchful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have' gives VE, the contraction in 'I've'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being watchful and paying close heed is being heedful and focused.

clue.text: Some diner terribly disinclined to move

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A dreadful diner is too lazy to get up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' looks like an anagram signal but is just part of the hiding text.
explanation.definitionFit: Something motionless or sluggish lacks the urge or power to stir.

clue.text: Ebb and flow restricted, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word for restricted is to be taken by its sound

parts.note: restricted, bound or tethered means tied

explanation.surface: Coming and going is limited, apparently.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea's twice-daily rise and fall is its tidal movement.

clue.text: What you see with "apple's"? It's upsetting to a shopper!

indicators.note: upsetting means knocking over, so these letters are tipped into a new order

explanation.surface: A badly punctuated shop sign irritates a customer.
explanation.walkthrough: The greengrocer's apostrophe ('apple's' for 'apples') is the joke; 'upsetting' rearranges TO A SHOPPER.
explanation.definitionFit: The punctuation mark wrongly inserted before the s in a plural on a grocer's sign.
